extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated power sector entities, and other stakeholders (industry, NGOs) engaged in implementing or commenting on EPA section 111(d) emission guidelines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rationale for selecting the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal-fired electric generating units (EGUs) under CAA section 111, including subcategorization by operating horizon and related monitoring/reporting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that source must transfer CO2 to an entity that reports under the GHGRP
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires that EGUs that capture CO2 in order to meet the applicable emission standard report in accordance with the GHGRP requirements of 40 CFR part 98, including subpart PP; if the CO2 is injected off site, the EGU must transfer the captured CO2 to a facility that reports in accordance with the requirements of 40 CFR part 98, subpart RR or subpart VV (or to a facility that has received an innovative technology waiver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GHGRP subpart RR and subpart VV provide monitoring and reporting mechanisms to quantify CO2 storage and to identify, quantify, and address potential leakage. UIC Class VI sequestration wells are required to report under subpart RR. Facilities with UIC Class II wells can opt-in to subpart RR by submitting an MRV plan. Subpart VV applies to facilities that conduct enhanced recovery using ISO 27916 unless they have opted into subpart RR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated (technology demonstration standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology is 'adequately demonstrated' if there is evidence of operation at scale, wide applicability, and available infrastructure (e.g., CCS has been operated at commercial scale, pipeline transport and geological storage are proven, and multiple projects exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on evidence such as commercial-scale operation (Boundary Dam, Petra Nova), long histories of CO2 pipelines and storage, numerous operating and under-construction projects, applicability of capture methods (e.g., amine solvent-based capture for post-combustion flue gas), and feasibility of source-to-sink logistics. The agency may draw upon testing at individual commercial-scale sources and extrapolate to related sources when specific technological improvements can be identified and reasonably expected to achieve the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost (reasonableness of costs to achieve reductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining BSER, EPA must take into account the cost of achieving the reduction; costs should be evaluated on $/ton CO2 reduced and $/MWh bases and account for factors that affect costs to the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may account for tax incentives (e.g., IRC section 45Q) because costs should reflect costs to the source. Cost assessments should consider amortization periods, source-specific transport and storage costs, capacity factors, and model projections (e.g., IPM). The rule evaluates whether costs are comparable to prior control cost metrics and presents examples (e.g., average total costs for CCS with 12-year amortization and 80% capacity factor were presented as −$5/ton CO2 and −$4/MWh for a specified fleet). Cost reasonableness may vary with remaining operating horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: BSER selection must consider potential non-air quality health/environmental impacts and the energy requirements of the control technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CCS, EPA considered flue gas pretreatment needs (removal of SO2 and PM), solvent degradation/loss, and regulatory frameworks (PHMSA for pipeline safety; UIC Class VI and GHGRP subpart RR for geologic sequestration protection) to conclude impacts can be mitigated. Energy requirements (steam and electricity demands of capture plants) and systemic impacts on generation and the energy sector should be evaluated; incentives (like 45Q) can alter net generation and therefore energy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emission reduction effectiveness / unit-level reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude of emission reductions achievable at the unit level is a key criterion in selecting BSER (e.g., 90% capture CCS yields substantially greater unit-level reductions than 40% natural gas co-firing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compares percent reductions in stack emission rates (example: 40% co-firing achieves ~16% stack emission rate reduction while 90% CCS achieves ~88.4% reduction) and weighs greater unit-level reductions heavily when technologies are otherwise comparable on cost and other BSER factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture rate and its implications for effectiveness and economics
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen capture rate (e.g., 90% for CCS) must balance emissions removed and economic considerations; lower capture (partial CCS) may remove fewer emissions and be less economical due to lost economies of scale and reduced tax credit benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes economies of scale favor higher capture rates and that tax credit incentives (IRC section 45Q) are tied to the amount of CO2 sequestered, so lower capture rates would receive less tax credit and likely have higher net costs per ton. EPA assessed that 90% capture both achieves high absolute emissions reductions and is cost-reasonable after accounting for credits and amortization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization criteria (distinguishing classes, types, sizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may create subcategories within a source category when sources have characteristics relevant to the BSER (e.g., operating horizon/remaining useful life affects cost reasonableness of controls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcategorization can be based on cost of controls, operating horizon (period a unit will continue to operate), load level, or fuel type—each affecting feasibility and cost reasonableness. EPA must set generally applicable BSERs for subcategories, while states retain authority to consider unit-specific RULOF in applying standards. The agency used operating-horizon subcategories (imminent/near/medium/long-term) to reflect that many units plan to cease operation and that amortization periods affect annualized costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation timeline and amortization period for cost reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost reasonableness assessments must consider the time over which capital costs can be amortized relative to the source's expected remaining operation (e.g., CCS is more cost-reasonable for units operating more than 7 years after compliance date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated costs for different amortization periods and used implementation/compliance dates (e.g., CCS evaluated with compliance date January 1, 2032; co-firing implementation date January 1, 2030) to determine which technologies are reasonable for long-term vs medium-term units. Shorter operating horizons increase annualized cost and may make capital-intensive technologies unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated for natural gas co-firing (technical feasibility evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas co-firing at 40% of annual heat input is adequately demonstrated for coal-fired steam generating units based on existing practice and technical capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites boiler modifications (installation of gas burners, fuel supply lines, duct modifications), operational experience (many plants already consume natural gas; examples of units co-firing at or above 40% and even 60% on an hourly basis), and natural gas pipeline network capacity and potential lateral construction. The assessment considers possible slight changes in efficiency and net heat rate, and evaluates pipeline development requirements (length, size, location) and associated costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: RULOF/state-specific flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: States may consider remaining useful life (RULOF) and unit-specific factors to establish less stringent standards of performance for individual sources even where EPA has set a generally applicable BSER for a subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA clarifies that setting subcategories does not preclude states from invoking RULOF in the state plan process; state authority to consider RULOF is premised on factors relevant to individual units (costs, technical feasibility) and distinct from EPA's generally applicable BSER determinations. Procedures for states' consideration of RULOF are detailed elsewhere in the preamble (section X.C.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible evidence and legal precedent for demonstrating adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may rely on data from individual commercial-scale sources, testing, and projections and may extrapolate testing at one kind of source to related sources when justified by identifiable technological improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent allows EPA to make an adequate demonstration finding based on commercial-scale projects (Boundary Dam, Petra Nova), historical infrastructure and transport data, and identification of technological improvements that can be expected to achieve the standard. The D.C. Circuit has accepted such extrapolations and projections in establishing achievable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of advancements in control technology as a consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing BSER may consider whether a determination promotes advancements in control technology for the pollutant (CO2 in this case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that determining CCS as BSER promotes advancements in CO2 control technology, and that such promotion is a relevant consideration under section 111 when weighing systems of emission reduction.
